transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

Here's what I take the problem to be, from your own words and your export.

**The real decision.** You are not forecasting "bookings" for their own sake — you are choosing a number per destination that minimises a lopsided cost: too few and you pay roughly three times the price for freelancers, too many and you pay a small fee per guide you don't use. That means the useful answer is not a single average, it's a level of demand you're comfortable reserving against. A model judged on plain accuracy will get you a different number than one judged on what a miss actually costs.

**What your table says.** 1,500 bookings from 2025-01-01 to 2026-02-24, travel dates reaching 2026-08-16, five live destinations (Paris 317, Bangkok 304, Dubai 302, London 283, Istanbul 282) plus 12 rows marked "TEST" that look like junk. 343 bookings were cancelled. Crucially, people book far ahead: 494 came in 60–119 days out and 514 at 120 days or more. So by the time you write to your partners, a good part of the month you're reserving for is *already in your file*. That is my main difference from the obvious approach: instead of a time series on monthly totals, I'd build the forecast as what's already on the books for that month, plus the arrivals still to come, net of expected cancellations, per destination.

**Plan:** clean the export (drop TEST rows, price is text) → measure the booking curve so we know how much is known at decision time → fit and validate the forecast against simple baselines → turn the forecast into a reserve number using your cost split → a monthly refresh you can run yourself.

To tune the last step I need two things from you: what the fee for one unused guide is relative to one guide's normal price, and which day of the month you lock the reservation in.

The two cards below are the quick first step and the standing dashboard; the forecast model itself is the third route and the one I'd recommend. Which do you want me to start?

[DCLab drew a chart with its numbers table and a chart with its numbers table above this message]

The booking curve is shown in two charts, and it changes the shape of the problem.

**How people book you.** Across the whole export (1,488 real bookings once the 12 "TEST" rows are out), arrivals spread like this: 108 at 0–14 days before travel, 122 at 15–29, 254 at 30–59, 238 at 60–89, 253 at 90–119, 513 at 120–179, and nothing beyond 180.

**What that means for your reservation.** When you write to partners about the month after next, roughly two-thirds of that month's demand is already sitting in your file, destination by destination: at 60+ days Bangkok 93, Dubai 86, London 86, Paris 83, Istanbul 75, against late arrivals Bangkok 24, Dubai 13, London 22, Paris 25, Istanbul 15. So the model DCLab should build is not a blind time series on monthly totals; it anchors on the bookings already taken and predicts only the remaining arrivals and the cancellations. That is a much easier, much more accurate forecast than the one your director asked for in the abstract.

**Two cautions from the same charts.** Monthly net bookings per destination run roughly 6–23, so a miss of 2–3 guides is a big proportional error — and the free-cancellation flag is useless for guessing who cancels: 22.6% cancel without it versus 23.3% with it. Cancellation by destination is real, though (Paris 18.9%, Istanbul 19.9%, up to Dubai 26.2%), so the net factor should be per destination.

To turn a forecast into a reservation number I need your cost split: roughly what does one unused reserved guide cost you compared with what you would pay a freelancer for that same guide — a tenth of it, a third? That ratio is what decides how far above the average forecast you should reserve.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

I chose the forecast model your director asked for, built the way the booking curve points to. What DCLab will build: one row per destination per target month, with the decision date fixed near month-end for the month after next. Only bookings taken **on or before** that day count as features, so the model gets the count already on the books for the target month and has to predict the rest — remaining arrivals plus the cancellation rate, which differs by destination (Paris 18.9% to Dubai 26.2%). That as-of rule is the one thing that makes or breaks it; without it the model would score beautifully and still be useless. How it will be judged: against two honest baselines — "what's already booked for that month" and "same destination, same month last year" — on the last three travel months it can see. I'll report error in guides per destination-month, not just a percentage. One assumption you should know about: you gave me the shortage cost (about 3x a guide's price) but not the fee for an unused guide. I've assumed it's roughly a quarter of a guide's price, which puts the right reservation near the **85th percentile** of predicted demand rather than the average — reserving high, because being short costs far more than being idle. Tell me the real fee and I'll re-set that percentile. DCLab is checking the remaining build requirements now; I'll come back with the numbers once it has run.

Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

What I heard: the board wants a segmentation, but the real job is allocation — six named groups that tell each campaign manager which of three emails a customer gets, once and only once. So I'd judge segments by whether they separate *who to move, who to keep, who to welcome*, not just by whether they look tidy on a slide.

Your table already says a few useful things. The segment you record today hardly separates anything: business churns next month at 14.6% and consumer at 18.1%, so it won't carry a board story. Plan and spend do most of the work: basic 603 customers at 22.4% churn and 19.22 average spend, plus 369 at 11.1% and 48.41, premium 228 at 14.5% and 89.39. The welcome pool is small and clearly defined — 53 customers with tenure of 3 months or less out of 1,200 — and 144 carry three or more support tickets in 90 days.

How I'd build it, in steps:
1. Group the 1,200 customers on behaviour (tenure, spend, tickets, plan, city), five or six groups.
2. Profile every group: size, average spend, churn next month, share on a lower plan than their spend suggests — that's upgrade headroom.
3. Name each group for the slide, then map each one to exactly one campaign, with a "no campaign" bucket so nobody gets two.
5. Deliver the names plus one row per customer with segment and campaign, ready to load.

I'm assuming churned_next_month = 1 means they left the month after the snapshot, and monthly_spend is recurring revenue. Tell me if either is wrong.

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a company that sells accounting software to small firms. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

You've described a scoring model that didn't necessarily get worse — the world under it changed three times at once, and your manager is proposing a fix that can't address any of them.

What I understood: since summer the *mix* of leads changed (partner marketplace), since August the *inputs* changed (new CRM, two scored fields no longer collected), and the *definition of the outcome* changed (trial start instead of first payment). Any one of those makes top-ranked leads feel worse to a salesperson who is now calling people who start trials cheaply and pay rarely. A bigger model trained on a moving target just fits the mess more accurately.

How I'd work, then:

1. **Freeze "worse" in numbers.** Old score, per lead, by month since spring: hit rate per score decile under *both* definitions (trial started, first payment). If top-decile payment rate is flat while trial rate jumped, the complaint is partly definitional — stop here and change the score, not the model.
2. **Split by source** — marketplace vs your own traffic, same decile table. This usually explains most of the drop.
3. **Audit the two dropped fields**: what the scorer feeds them now (null, default, imputed) and whether the score distribution shifted in August. This is a bug check before a modelling check.
4. **Rebuild one consistent label** per lead from the raw event dates, and agree with finance and sales what the score should rank. I'm assuming both dates still exist somewhere; if so, the clean answer is often trial-likelihood *weighted by* payment likelihood.
5. **Only then retrain** — old model vs a plain logistic baseline vs the larger one, temporal holdout of the last three months, judged on decile payment rate and calibration, not AUC alone.

I'd do 1–3 before writing any training code. Here's how you might want DCLab to start.

Can you export the old training set plus every lead since (one row per lead, with score, source, CRM date, and both event dates if they exist) and share the table here? Then I can run steps 1–3 on the real numbers rather than on your description.

choices.what: On your exported leads, measure what actually degraded: conversion by lead source and by month, the score distribution before and after the August CRM move, top-decile hit rate under both definitions (trial start and first payment), and how the two dropped form fields changed. You get: Attribution of the autumn drop between the new marketplace traffic, the missing fields, and the label change - with numbers your manager can read. Trade-off: A bigger model cannot undo any of the three causes, and retraining now would bury them; the sales team may wait a while for a fix. Effort: Small - one export and a handful of queries.

choices.what: I walk through the failure as three separate drifts (label, schema/source, population), the standard order to test them in, what each fix costs, and how to answer your manager's 'bigger model' proposal without losing the argument or the quarter. You get: A second reading of your situation in writing, so the next move is chosen deliberately rather than being the manager's default. Trade-off: It reasons from your description, not your numbers, so it can name the likely cause but cannot prove which one dominates for you. Effort: Small - a written brief you can forward.

choices.what: Rebuild the model on one agreed target with a temporal holdout (last three months untouched), compared against the old model and against a plain logistic baseline, judged by decile hit rate rather than only AUC. You get: Whether extra size and features really buy anything, and a model that can score leads whose two missing fields are absent. Trade-off: If the label change explains most of the drop, you will have trained a better model on a moving definition of converted. Effort: Medium to large, and only sound after the lead history is harmonised onto one label.

transcript.text: Diagnose the drift first (no retraining)

Drift diagnosis is started. Nothing gets retrained; you'll get numbers that say which of your three breaks did the damage.

**What to export** — one row per lead, old training set and every lead since, unioned with a `period` flag:
`lead_id`, `lead_created_at` (the *original* pre-migration date if the new CRM back-filled it, keep both), `source`/channel, `crm_instance`, the **logged production score with its model version and scoring timestamp** (not recomputed — recomputing erases the drift you're testing), the two dropped form fields as they existed for old leads, whatever firmographics you still collect, `trial_start_date`, `first_payment_date`, plan/amount, current status, sales disposition + its date.

**The four checks, in order:**

1. **Score distribution drift.** Null rate of the two dropped fields by month, and a PSI-style shift of the score by month, before vs after August. If the fields now arrive as null/default, the model is scoring every lead against a feature it no longer has — that alone reorders the top decile, and it's a bug, not decay.
2. **Label change.** Top-decile hit rate per month under *both* definitions. If trial rate rose while payment rate held flat, the complaint is partly definitional and the answer is a new score target, not a bigger model.
3. **Mix.** Same decile table split by source. Marketplace leads will almost certainly have their own shape, and pooling them with your own traffic moves the average without the model changing at all.
4. **Seasonality control.** Each month against the same month last year, on cohorts with equal follow-up so recent months aren't unfairly marked down.

One thing I need from you to make step 1 work: does the new CRM keep the score per lead since August, or was scoring interrupted by the migration?
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

Decided and going ahead. Here's the design, with the calls you'd have made me take. A flat top decile with good mid-deciles is a ranking failure; a uniform slide is a base-rate failure, and those have different fixes. **Check 1 — the dropped fields (cheapest, most likely a bug).** Null/default rate of the two fields per month, and the score distribution per month across the August break. If inputs went null and the scorer filled a default, every post-August lead gets scored on a feature it no longer has, and the top decile is being chosen by whatever's left. That's a hotfix, not a retrain — and retraining first would bake the bug into the new model. **Check 2 — the label change.** Top-decile payment rate vs trial rate per month. If trials jumped and payments held, the sales team is being handed people who convert easily into something they don't buy. Finance's definition changed the target; the score didn't decay. **Check 3 — the marketplace.** Same decile table split by source. Two different causes look alike here: marketplace leads may be genuinely worse, or they may be *misranked* because the model never saw that traffic. I'm also adding reach rate (contacted, connected, dispositioned) by source — a sales team saying "the top leads are worse" sometimes means "I can't get hold of them," which no model fixes. Seasonality alone moves small-firm accounting purchases after a fiscal year end. **What you get:** one page ranking the causes by share of the drop, saying for each whether retraining would fix it, and a recommendation. If checks 1–3 explain most of it, my advice will be to fix the pipeline and the target, and retrain only on a rebuilt payment label with source and post-August features — a bigger model is the wrong tool for all three.

transcript.text: I am the credit risk manager at a consumer lender that finances phone and appliance purchases in shops. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. We have about 60,000 past loans with the application form, the bureau score and whether the loan defaulted within 12 months, and I can export them next week. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more. The model would decide each new application automatically at the shop counter. How should I go about it?

What you've described is not mainly a modelling problem — it's a missing-labels problem, and that's what should drive the design.

You have 12-month outcomes only for the 40% the rulebook let through. A model trained on those applicants and then asked to judge everyone, including the types the rulebook turned away, has never seen half the population it will decide on. The naive version quietly re-learns your underwriters' blind spots and scores beautifully in testing. Two further constraints follow from "automatic at the shop counter": every decline needs a stated reason, and the applicant mix and bureau behaviour will drift, so validation must be out-of-time, never a random split.

The plan I'd run:

1. Fix the target and the windows. 12-month default on loans matured at least 12 months; train on older cohorts, test on the newest ones only.
2. Baseline the rulebook first. Score the human decision itself on those rows and look at default rates by score band. If the rulebook already ranks the approved population well, the model's real upside is in the rejected group, not better sorting.
3. Model the 60,000, judged on ranking and calibration in the newest cohort, then use the forms and bureau scores you kept for rejects to estimate how that unseen group behaves.
4. Turn the score into a policy: expected loss versus margin per score band, and a cut-off that hits the approval rate management wants at a loss rate you accept.
5. Buy the missing labels: run shadow-mode on live applications, and randomise a small slice of borderline rejects so you observe their real defaults instead of inferring them forever. Whether governance will allow that slice is the open fork.

The three options below differ in how far you go before next week's export arrives. Which one fits how management wants to be shown this?

You build once you send the file next week. You get: A plan you can take to management and your board, and an export spec so the data arrives usable first time. Trade-off: No numbers yet — the design is only tested once real data runs. Effort: Short: one round, then the build.

choices.what: A default model on the 60,000 funded loans, trained on older cohorts and tested only on the most recent matured ones, scored side by side with your current rulebook decision on the same applications. You get: AUC/Kolmogorov–Smirnov, default rate and approvals at matched risk — evidence the model actually beats the rulebook rather than just predicting well in sample. Trade-off: It measures only the population you already approved; the reject side stays unproven. Effort: Medium — needs the export and about 12-month-old labels.

You get: A decision rule that answers management's real question — how many extra approvals, at what expected loss and profit. Trade-off: Needs cost, revenue and loss-tolerance figures from finance before it means anything. Effort: Longest, and depends on option 2 running first.

Good — blueprint now, build the moment the export lands. Here is what to design against, and what to make sure the export contains.

**What the decision really is.** Not "who defaults" but "who do we approve that the rulebook would have declined, at a loss rate management signs off on." The model is one input to a policy. Until you know the default rate on the approved book by cohort, the size of the prize is unknown — so the blueprint's money figures (base rate, cost of one wrong approve, margin per performing loan) are placeholders, deliberately not filled in.

**Minimum data the export needs.** Per loan: application date, disbursement date, decision (approve/decline) and the rulebook reason code, bureau score as captured at decision time, the raw form fields as the underwriter saw them, loan amount and term, product/merchant, and for funded loans a month-by-month performance flag plus the matured-12-months default label and amount lost. The two things people forget: the decision date, without which out-of-time validation is impossible, and the *features as they were at decision time* — never refreshed bureau scores or later status fields, those leak.

**The leakage traps to design out.** Anything post-disbursement (early-payment-behaviour fields, collection notes, settled flags) must be dropped before training. Rejects have no label — leave them unlabelled, never coded "non-default", or the model learns that declining is safe. And split by time, not randomly: oldest cohorts train, newest cohorts test.

**Build plan once the file arrives.** Define the label by maturity, not origination. Score the rulebook itself as a challenger model — if the humans already rank the approved book well, the model's value is in the rejected region. Train a scorecard or gradient-boosted model on 60,000 rows, judged on ranking (Gini/AUC), calibration by score band, and reason-code stability, all on the newest cohorts only. Then reject inference on the declines' form and bureau data, and a cut-off chosen from expected loss versus margin, not an accuracy number. Stop and go back to the drawing board if the model cannot beat the rulebook's out-of-time Gini — replacing a working rulebook with a score that can't beat it is a governance failure, not a win.

One thing decides the last two steps, so tell me which it is: will your governance function let you fund a small randomised slice of borderline rejects so their true default rate is measured, or must the model be built from approved loans alone, relying on reject inference plus shadow-mode scoring at the counter?

When the export is ready, upload it and say "build it" and I'll start the project against this blueprint.

1. Boundary: features only as they stood at the counter on application day — form fields, bureau score as captured, requested amount, product and merchant. Judge on Gini/AUC plus expected utility at the approval rate management wants, with calibration by score band and reason-code stability, all on the out-of-time cohorts. 5. transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

## What the problem is

Your real decision is not just “how many bookings will we receive?” but “how many guides should we reserve for each destination for the month you are planning?”

- **Decision behind it:** choose a guide reservation quantity per destination for the upcoming planning month, knowing that too few guides forces expensive last-minute freelancers, while too many guides causes idle reservation fees.
- **Who uses the result:** you, the operations lead, and possibly the local partners you brief. The model output should be an actionable reservation number, not only a booking forecast.
- **Unit:** ideally **guides per destination per target month**. If the relationship between bookings and guides is not yet defined, the practical unit is **confirmed bookings that will need guide coverage** for that destination-month.
- **Moment it concerns:** the target month is the planning month you are reserving for, and you should make the forecast using only information available at the decision moment. Because your export goes up to late February 2026, any future travel month in the data is partially observed, not final.
- **What is known:** you have booking-level records with booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time, price, free-cancellation flag, cancellation flag, and customer identifier. You also know the cost asymmetry: under-reserving is expensive because freelancers cost about three times more, while over-reserving has a smaller per-guide penalty.
- **What is not known:** how many bookings require how many guests or guides, guide capacity rules, minimum guide requirements, exact cancellation deadlines, no-show behavior, exact guide reservation cost, exact freelancer cost, and how much usable history exists for each destination. The table schema also raises a few data issues: price is listed as categorical, cancelled is listed as numeric, and identifiers may not be useful as raw categories.

A booking forecast is useful only if it is converted into confirmed guide demand. A booking may be cancelled, may not need a guide, or may belong to a group that shares guide coverage. Therefore, the cleanest target is expected guide need per destination for the reservation month.

---

## Approaches that could solve it

### 1. No model: simple reservation rule

Use historical patterns directly: same destination-month from prior history, recent moving averages, or current bookings for the target month adjusted by a manual safety buffer.

**Cost:** very low. Quick to build, easy to explain, and uses little data.

**What it gives:** a baseline. It is often surprisingly strong when data are small or destinations are few. Because under-reserving costs much more than over-reserving, a simple rule can be made safer by adding a buffer based on your judgment of the cost asymmetry.

**Risk:** it may miss growth, seasonality shifts, channel changes, cancellation changes, or destination-level differences.

---

### 2. Aggregate destination-month booking forecast

Build a dataset where each training example is one destination-month: count past confirmed bookings that needed guide coverage, then forecast the same quantity for future destination-months.

Possible models: simple regression, Poisson-style count model, negative-binomial count model, or gradient-boosted trees.

**Cost:** moderate. Needs feature engineering and careful history.

**What it gives:** a forecast of bookings per destination-month. It can learn seasonality, trends, destination differences, channel mix, nationality mix, price patterns, and cancellation history.

**Risk:** it may still be too coarse for your exact decision moment because future months in the data are only partially booked. If you train only on completed past months, you may underuse the bookings already made for the target month.

---

### 3. Lead-time completion forecast

Because each row has booking date, travel date, and lead time, you can estimate how final bookings for a future month will build over time. For each destination, you look at:

- bookings already made for the target month,
- historical lead-time patterns,
- share of final bookings that usually arrive at different lead-time intervals,
- seasonality and destination-specific booking behavior.

Then you project the remaining late bookings and add them to the already-known bookings.

**Cost:** moderate to high, depending on how stable the lead-time patterns are.

**What it gives:** a forecast aligned with the actual decision moment. It directly answers: “For the reservation month, what do we already know from bookings made so far, and how much more should we expect to arrive?”

**Risk:** lead-time patterns can change because of channel behavior, holidays, pricing changes, or destination popularity. Rare destinations may have too little history for stable curves.

---

### 4. Per-booking machine-learning model

Predict booking-level outcomes, such as cancellation or guide need, then aggregate expected bookings per destination-month.

**Cost:** high. Needs careful data cleaning, feature selection, and validation.

**What it gives:** potentially detailed estimates of confirmed demand, especially if cancellation and guide need depend on free cancellation, nationality, channel, price, or lead time.

**Risk:** for only 1,500 rows, this may overfit and may be unnecessarily complex. The decision is aggregate guide capacity, so a booking-level model may not improve the actual reservation quality.

---

### 5. Decision-aware reservation model

First forecast the range of likely guide demand, then choose the reservation number by balancing under-reservation cost and over-reservation cost.

**Cost:** moderate. It needs forecast uncertainty and your cost rules.

**What it gives:** the actual output you need: recommended guides per destination, not just expected bookings. Because freelancers cost about three times more than reserved guides, the recommended reservation should usually be above the central expected demand, but the exact safety level depends on the real cost of idle guides and the distribution of demand.

**Risk:** without uncertainty and cost inputs, this can become arbitrary. The key is to make the model cost-aware rather than only accuracy-aware.

---

## Recommended approach

I recommend a **lead-time-aware destination-month demand forecast, converted into guide reservations using the cost asymmetry**.

That means:

1. Forecast final confirmed bookings, or confirmed guide demand, for each destination in the reservation month.
2. Use current bookings for that target month plus historical lead-time completion patterns.
3. Adjust for cancellations, free-cancellation behavior, and destination characteristics.
4. Convert the forecast into a guide reservation number.
5. Select a reservation quantity that reflects that under-reserving is much more costly than over-reserving.

If the history is too sparse for machine learning, stop the model and use the no-model baseline. A simple robust rule is often better than a fragile machine-learning model when data are small.

---

## Step-by-step plan

### Step 1: Define the real target

Before building anything, decide what the model should predict.

Best target: **confirmed guide units needed per destination for the target travel month**.

If that mapping is not available, use the next best target: **confirmed non-cancelled bookings requiring guide coverage per destination for the target travel month**.

This step needs:

- guide capacity rules,
- guests-per-guide assumptions if needed,
- minimum guide requirements,
- cancellation policy,
- no-show handling if applicable,
- definition of “confirmed” demand.

If you do not know these yet, build the forecast on confirmed non-cancelled bookings and keep the guide conversion as a manual overlay.

---

### Step 2: Clean and interpret the booking table

Prepare the table as booking history, not as a single snapshot.

Needed checks:

- Parse `booking_date` and `travel_date` as dates.
- Confirm that `booking_date` occurs before or on `travel_date`.
- Check whether `lead_time_days` matches the difference between travel and booking dates.
- Inspect `cancelled`; even though the schema says numeric, it may be a flag.
- Decide how to use `price`. The schema says categorical, but it may be a price tier or a mis-typed numeric field. If numeric, use it carefully; if categorical, treat it as price band.
- Do not use `booking_id` or `customer_id` as raw categories unless you convert them into meaningful features, such as repeat-customer behavior or customer-specific booking history.
- Remove duplicates only if they are true duplicates. Otherwise, keep them if each row is a separate booking.

This step needs only the table itself plus quick validation queries.

---

### Step 3: Build historical completed months

Create a label table for months that are fully observed.

For each destination and travel month, compute:

- total bookings,
- cancelled bookings,
- confirmed bookings,
- confirmed bookings that require guide coverage,
- cancellation rate,
- channel mix,
- nationality mix,
- lead-time distribution,
- average or banded price,
- free-cancellation mix.

Only use months where enough time has passed for final cancellation status and booking completion. Since your export is up to late February 2026, months near the end of the dataset may be incomplete and should not be treated as final unless enough lead time has elapsed.

This step gives the historical “answer key” for model evaluation.

---

### Step 4: Build point-in-time training examples

This is the most important modeling detail.

For each possible historical decision moment, create a training row for the destination and target month you were trying to reserve.

For each destination-target month:

- use only bookings with `booking_date` available at that decision moment,
- include current partial bookings for the target month,
- include features known before the decision moment,
- label the row with the final confirmed bookings or guide demand observed later.

This prevents leakage. A model should not see cancellations or bookings that had not happened yet at the time of the reservation decision.

This step needs a rolling history of decision months. If you do not have enough destination-month observations, use pooled models or simple rules instead of destination-specific models.

---

### Step 5: Create features that match your actual decision

Useful features:

- destination identity,
- target month or seasonal marker,
- prior-year same destination-month,
- recent trend in that destination,
- current known bookings for the target month at the decision moment,
- lead-time buckets: how many bookings usually arrive early, mid, or late,
- channel mix,
- nationality mix,
- cancellation rate by destination, channel, and season,
- share of bookings with free cancellation,
- price band,
- lead time distribution,
- whether the destination is growing, flat, or declining,
- whether the destination has stable guide demand or erratic demand.

Do not over-engineer. The most helpful features are usually:

1. already booked for the target month,
2. historical same-season behavior,
3. lead-time pattern,
4. destination-specific trend.

---

### Step 6: Start with a no-model baseline

Build a transparent baseline first.

Possible baseline:

- take the same destination-month from prior history,
- adjust it with the recent trend in that destination,
- add the bookings already observed for the target month,
- project likely remaining bookings using a simple lead-time completion rule,
- subtract likely cancellations,
- convert to guide units,
- apply a conservative buffer because freelancer hiring costs about three times more.

This baseline should be the first thing you test. If a model cannot beat this baseline, the model is not earning its complexity.

---

### Step 7: Choose the model type

If enough destination-month history exists, use a simple count-based model.

Good options:

- **Poisson or negative-binomial regression** for destination-month booking counts.
- **Regularized linear model** with destination and seasonal features.
- **Gradient-boosted count model** if non-linear patterns are clear and data volume supports it.
- **Hierarchical or pooled model** if destinations are sparse; this lets rare destinations borrow strength from similar destinations.

If data are too sparse, do not force a complex model. Use:

- destination-level manual rules,
- simple lead-time completion,
- pooled seasonal averages,
- a human-adjusted forecast.

The model should output not just an average but also uncertainty, such as an expected level plus an upper and lower forecast range. Uncertainty matters because your reservation decision is asymmetric.

---

### Step 8: Convert bookings into guide reservations

This step needs your operating rule.

If guide need is linear, for example a fixed guests-per-guide ratio, divide forecast confirmed demand by that capacity rule and round up to whole guides.

If guide need has minimums, for example one guide even for small groups, apply those rules.

If the guide mapping is uncertain, forecast confirmed bookings first and let you manually convert to guides each month. That is safer than hiding the mapping inside the model.

Because under-reserving costs about three times more than over-reserving, the final reservation should not simply be the central forecast. It should include a safety margin.

A useful approach:

1. Forecast a central expected demand.
2. Produce an upper forecast range.
3. Simulate monthly outcomes across history.
4. Test different reservation levels.
5. Choose the level that minimizes the combined cost of idle guide fees and last-minute freelancer hires.

If you cannot simulate exact costs yet, use a conservative upper range and document the assumption. Do not just use the average.

---

### Step 9: Validate with rolling backtests

Do not randomly split the data. Time series and booking forecasts need point-in-time validation.

For each historical decision moment:

- pretend you only know data up to that moment,
- forecast the destination-month guide demand,
- wait for the actual final result,
- compare forecast to actual,
- compare reservation decision to actual guide need,
- measure cost implications.

Evaluation metrics:

- forecast error by destination,
- forecast bias: are you systematically overforecasting or underforecasting,
- performance on high-volume versus low-volume destinations,
- performance on stable versus volatile destinations,
- performance on popular months versus off-season months,
- number of last-minute freelancer hires avoided or created,
- idle-guide fees incurred,
- overall reservation cost simulated over history.

Compare every candidate model to the no-model baseline. A good model should beat the baseline on error and, more importantly, on reservation cost.

---

### Step 10: Add human review before the model decides

Because this affects partner reservations and cost, the first live output should be a recommendation, not an automatic instruction.

Monthly output should include:

- destination,
- target month,
- central expected confirmed bookings,
- recommended guide reservation,
- uncertainty range,
- key drivers,
- manual override field,
- last-minute booking trend,
- cancellation trend,
- comparison with prior month.

You can override the model for:

- special events,
- known partner changes,
- new marketing campaigns,
- channel outages,
- price changes,
- destination closures or openings,
- unusual customer behavior.

The model should support judgment, not replace it.

---

## When to stop and when to escalate

Stop building a more complex model if:

- the no-model baseline performs almost as well,
- the model does not improve reservation cost in backtests,
- destinations have too little history,
- the model is hard to explain to partners,
- it depends on features that will not be reliably available each month,
- it uses information that would not have been known at the reservation decision moment.

Escalate the data problem if:

- cancelled values are not clear,
- price is mis-typed and not interpretable,
- bookings for future months are incomplete and lead-time patterns are unstable,
- there are too few fully observed destination-months,
- guide capacity rules are unknown,
- no-shows are material but not recorded.

The practical stop condition is: you have a transparent destination-month forecast, a conversion rule to guides, and a backtest showing the reservation policy lowers expected total cost compared with your current process.

---

## Assumptions I am making

These are assumptions, not facts from your message:

- `booking_date` records when the booking was made.
- `travel_date` records the service month for guide planning.
- A cancelled booking does not require a reserved guide.
- The final guide need depends on confirmed bookings, not raw bookings.
- Guide need can be converted from confirmed bookings using a business rule, even if that rule is currently manual.
- Future-month bookings in the export are only partially observed and need lead-time projection.
- `cancelled` contains a meaningful status value.
- `price` may be numeric despite being labeled categorical.
- The table contains enough history for at least some destination-month patterns, though possibly not enough for complex machine learning.
- The decision horizon is fixed: you forecast the reservation month using only information available before partners must be told how many guides to reserve.

**What the problem really is**

This is not only a “make clusters for the board” problem. It is a **campaign target-assignment problem**.

The decision is: **which customers should enter each of the three email campaign lists next quarter?**  
The users of the result are your campaign managers, who need a clear, repeatable way to put each customer into one segment and then decide whether that segment maps to:

- a welcome series for new customers,
- a retention/save campaign for people who look likely to leave,
- a higher-plan upsell campaign,
- or no targeted campaign.

The unit is **one customer per row**.  
The moment is **now, based on the customer’s current state before campaigns are sent**.

What is known from what you shared:

- The table has **1200 customer rows**.
- Each row has signup date, an already recorded segment, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether the customer churned next month.
- You need about **five or six named segments**.
- The team can run **at most three campaigns** next quarter.
- The same customer should not receive two campaigns.

What is not known from what you shared:

- The actual values or distributions of any column.
- Whether every customer has a reliable churn label.
- What the existing “segment” field means internally.
- Which plans are higher than which plans.
- What counts as “new” for the welcome series.
- Whether monthly spend is the best measure of value.
- Whether city or current segment should influence campaign choice.
- Whether there is past campaign-response data.

What I am assuming, separate from what you told me:

- `churned_next_month` is a clean enough outcome to train on.
- Some plan or spend signal can serve as a proxy for upgrade potential, even though the table does not show future plan upgrades.
- The existing `segment` field may be useful, but it could also overlap with the new segments, so it needs to be handled carefully.
- The campaign priority can be set by marketing, for example: new customer first, retention before upsell, etc.

---

### 1. No model at all: business rules

Create segments using simple rules, for example:

- New customers by signup date or tenure.
- Likely-to-leave customers by high support tickets and low tenure.
- Upsell candidates by plan or spend.
- Everyone else in stable or low-priority buckets.

**Cost:** very low.  
**What it gives:** transparent, easy to explain, fast.  
**Main weakness:** it may not be very precise, and it may not actually improve campaign choices. It may also feel like “not real AI” to the board.

---

### 2. Unsupervised segmentation / clustering

Run a clustering method on features like tenure, plan, spend, support tickets, and maybe churn behavior.

**Cost:** moderate.  
**What it gives:** data-driven groups, useful for storytelling.  
**Main weakness:** the clusters may not map neatly to your three campaigns. A cluster might contain both likely-to-leave customers and good upsell customers, which makes it hard for campaign managers.

This is often not the best choice here because your table already contains a useful outcome: `churned_next_month`.

---

### 3. Predictive churn model plus business segmentation

Build a model that estimates each customer’s likelihood of churning next month. Then use that churn risk together with business signals like plan, tenure, spend, and support tickets to create the final named segments.

**Cost:** moderate.  
**What it gives:** the most practical fit for your situation. You get:

- a risk score for retention campaigns,
- named segments for the board slide,
- customer lists campaign managers can use,
- and a way to keep segments mutually exclusive.

This is the approach I would recommend.
